newsitem.title: USA: Burundi's Buyoya says ex-president will leave soon.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's Buyoya says ex-president will leave soon.

text.p: Burundi's military leader expects his country's ousted president will soon leave the U.S. ambassador's residence where he sought refuge during last July's coup, according to Newsweek International magazine.

"I think he (Sylvestre Ntibantunganya) is going to go out (of the U.S. residence) now," military leader Pierre Buyoya told Newsweek in an interview released on Sunday that will be on the newstands on Monday.
Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army took power in a coup last July, installing ethnic-Tutsi Buyoya and ousting a freely elected Hutu government led by Ntibantunganya.
Fearing his life was in danger, Ntibantunganya sought refuge in the American ambassador's residence in the capital Bujumbura during the coup.

"He (Ntibantunganya) has been hostage of his own people. They have been telling him: 'Stay there, we are fighting for constitutional legality, we can come back to power. The embargo (against Burundi) is helping us'. I think now that illusion is over," Buyoya said.
African regional leaders eased sanctions on Burundi last week which were imposed on July 31 in response to the coup and the ousting of Ntibantunganya.
Buyoya reiterated earlier denials that Burundi along with Rwanda and Uganda was supporting the rebel movement in Zaire. "No, the Zairean conflict is really Zairean," he said.
The embattled Zairean government has accused Burundi in the past of sending its troops into Zaire to aid the rebellion.

Asked whether he thought Washington was supporting the Zairean rebels, Buyoya said: "I think the influence of external powers is evident. No African power is helping (rebel leader Laurent) Kabila more than some external powers," he said.

When asked to be more specific, Buyoya said the situation would probably become clearer in the coming weeks. "In Kabila's case what's most important is political support. He has his own means. What he needs is not monetary but political support."
